summary: This Structural Learning blog post by Paul Main (December 8, 2023) explains rote learning as a memorization technique based on repetition, covering its definition, classroom examples, techniques such as spaced repetition, and its advantages and disadvantages. It argues rote learning is useful for foundational facts like times tables, spelling and dates, but should be supplemented with critical thinking and meaningful learning. The page also lists five further-reading research papers and includes site navigation and a lead-capture form that are not part of the content.
one_line: A Structural Learning blog post explaining rote learning as memorization through repetition, its benefits, drawbacks, and role alongside critical thinking.
key_facts: The article 'Rote Learning' by Paul Main was published December 8, 2023 on the Structural Learning website.
Rote learning is defined as a memorization technique that involves repeating information over and over until it is committed to memory.
The article states rote learning is often criticized for not promoting deeper comprehension or critical thinking skills.
Examples of rote learning given include spelling games, repetition of the alphabet, memorizing multiplication tables, memory games, and multi-sensory rote learning.
Spaced repetition is described as a learning technique that involves spacing out review of material over increasing intervals of time.
The article lists advantages of rote learning including quick recall of facts, foundational knowledge, order and sequence, and retention of lists.
The article lists disadvantages of rote learning including superficial understanding, short-term retention, lack of engagement, and minimal critical thinking.
Types of knowledge suited to rote learning include times tables, spelling, historical dates, scientific terminology, geographical facts, and language vocabulary.
Medical professionals may benefit from rote learning when memorizing drug dosages or the symptoms of particular diseases.
The article cites R. Roche et al. (2009) on prolonged rote learning producing delayed memory facilitation in the hippocampus of the ageing human brain.
The article cites D. Michie (1968) on 'Memo' functions and machine learning, discussing a rote-learning facility that improves program efficiency.
The article cites Hell and Mahn (1997) finding that for experienced learners rote learning can be more effective than keyword mnemonics for foreign words.
The article cites Ross and Ross (1978) finding that imagery techniques are more effective than rote learning for multiple-associate learning in EMR children.
